cards.title: Before we start: moving day
cards.body: On moving day you carry a lamp into the new flat. Is it already standing there, or are you putting it there? German asks two different questions, Wo? and Wohin?, and the little word before the noun changes. You already know the idea from im Kino and ins Kino.
steps: You already know: Wir sind im Kino and Wir gehen ins Kino (chapter 6), and that the Bild hängt an der Wand (lesson 5).
New today: when you PUT something somewhere (Wohin?), the noun after in, auf, an and the other place words takes the accusative: an die Wand.
By the end you can: tell a helper where to stand, lay and hang every box, lamp and picture.

examples.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.en: The picture hangs on the wall.
examples.why: You know this already. It is there already (Wo?), so der Wand is dative.

examples.de: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
examples.en: I hang the picture on the wall.
examples.why: New today: I put it there (Wohin?), so der Wand becomes die Wand (accusative).

examples.en: We go to the cinema.
examples.why: You know this already: ins = in das, a movement (Wohin?).

cards.more: Think of a film. In one scene the lamp just sits on the table. That is a photo: nothing moves, so you ask Wo? In the next scene your hand carries the lamp to the table. That is a movie: something moves, so you ask Wohin? German gives the photo one ending (dem, der) and the movie another (den, die). In this lesson you learn the movie endings, step by step. You know most of them already, because der, die, das and den, die are old friends from the food chapter.

cards.title: Wo? or Wohin?: two questions, two cases
cards.lead: The intro showed a photo and a movie. On this card you learn the one question that decides everything, so you always know which ending to pick.
cards.body: After in, auf, an, neben, hinter, vor, unter, über and zwischen, ask a question. Wo? (no movement, it is there) means dative. Wohin? (movement, you put it there) means accusative. The question tells you the case.
steps: 1. Is the thing already there? Ask Wo? Use the dative: auf dem Tisch.
2. Are you moving it there? Ask Wohin? Use the accusative: auf den Tisch.
3. The little place word (in, auf, an …) stays the same. Only the article changes.

examples.en: We are in the cinema.
We go to the cinema.

examples.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.en: The picture hangs on the wall.

examples.de: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
examples.en: I hang the picture on the wall.
examples.why: Wohin? I put it there: accusative.

cards.more: Imagine a lamp. Step 1: is anybody moving it? No: it just sits there, so ask Wo? and use the dative (auf dem Tisch). Step 2: is a hand putting it there? Yes: ask Wohin? and use the accusative (auf den Tisch). You are not guessing the ending. You are asking the lamp one question. If you can say Where is it? it is Wo. If you can say Where to? it is Wohin.

deeper.text: In English the same split hides in two small words: we say in the cinema (being) and into the cinema (going). German keeps the same little word and changes the article instead. A good test: can you add the word to? If you can say to the wall, ask Wohin? and use the accusative.

example.en: Mira goes into the kitchen. (Wohin?)

cards.title: The accusative after the nine place words
cards.lead: You know that Wohin? means accusative. On this card you see exactly which articles change, and you will find that only one of the four changes.
cards.body: Only der-words change: dem becomes den. The die-words stay die, the das-words stay das, and the plural is die without the -n that the dative plural needed. So just the masculine form is new.

examples.en: Mira goes into the kitchen.
Ben goes to the cupboard.

examples.de: Die Kinder gehen in die Zimmer.
examples.en: The children go into the rooms.
examples.why: Plural: die, no -n on the noun.

examples.en: Leon goes to the table.

cards.more: Think of four people in a line. Three of them, die, das and the plural, simply stay as they are. Only der changes his hat: dem becomes den. Step 1: find the gender of the noun. Step 2: if it is a der-word, write den. Step 3: all others stay die or das. Step 4: in the plural, drop the -n that you added for the dative (an den Wänden becomes an die Wände).

deeper.text: Careful: mit, bei, zu, aus and von from chapter 7 are not in the group of nine. They always take the dative, even when something moves: Ich gehe zum Schrank, Ich komme aus der Küche. Only the nine two-way words switch to the accusative for Wohin?. So first check the word, then ask the question.

example.en: I go to the cupboard.

cards.title: stellen: put something standing up
cards.lead: Now you know the accusative. On this card you meet the first verb of moving, stellen, which is the partner of stehen from lesson 5.
cards.body: stehen means to stand (Wo?). stellen means to put something so that it stands (Wohin?). stehen is dative, stellen is accusative: Der Schrank steht an der Wand. Ich stelle den Schrank an die Wand. stellen is a regular verb: ich stelle, er stellt.

examples.de: Der Schrank steht an der Wand.
examples.en: The cupboard stands at the wall.

examples.de: Ich stelle den Schrank an die Wand.
examples.en: I put the cupboard at the wall.

examples.de: Mira stellt den Stuhl an den Tisch.
examples.en: Mira puts the chair at the table.

examples.de: Wir stellen die Lampe in die Ecke.
examples.en: We put the lamp in the corner.

cards.more: Picture a toy figure. Stehen is when the figure already stands on the shelf: it stands. Stellen is your hand putting the figure on the shelf: you stand it up. Step 1: if you only describe, use stehen and the dative. Step 2: if you do something with your hand, use stellen and the accusative. Step 3: stellen is a normal verb: ich stelle, du stellst, er stellt. Extra example: Anna stellt die Lampe auf den Tisch.

deeper.text: Stellen always needs something to put: a thing (the accusative object) and a place. Because of that it needs two parts in the sentence: what you put and where you put it. Stehen needs no object: it only says where something is. If a sentence has a thing you move, you probably need stellen.

example.de: Anna stellt das Sofa an das Fenster.
example.en: Anna puts the sofa at the window.

cards.title: legen and hängen
cards.lead: You can stand things up with stellen. On this card you learn the partners for lying and hanging things, so you can put every object in the right place.
cards.body: liegen (Wo?) has the partner legen (Wohin?): you lay something down. hängen is easy: it works for both. Das Bild hängt an der Wand (Wo?). Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand (Wohin?). legen is regular: ich lege, er legt.

examples.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The book lies on the table.

examples.de: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
examples.en: I lay the book on the table.

examples.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.en: The picture hangs on the wall.

examples.de: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
examples.en: I hang the picture on the wall.
examples.why: hängen, Wohin?: accusative. Same verb form.

cards.more: Three pairs, like three light switches. Switch 1: stehen is the state, stellen is the action. Switch 2: liegen is the state, legen is the action. Switch 3: hängen is the state and the action, but the word looks the same for both. Step 1: ask Wo? or Wohin? Step 2: choose the verb and the case. Step 3: say it. Extra example: Ben legt das Handy auf den Tisch.

deeper.text: There is a fourth pair: sitzen and setzen. sitzen says where a person sits (Wo?, dative); setzen means to sit someone or something down (Wohin?, accusative): Ich setze das Kind auf den Stuhl. Like stellen and legen, setzen has an e where sitzen has an i. The action verbs all need an object.

example.de: Ich setze das Kind auf den Stuhl.
example.en: I sit the child down on the chair.

cards.title: ins, ans, aufs: the short forms
cards.lead: You know the full accusative forms. On this card you learn how das-words shrink the little word and the article into one word, and how that differs from im and am.
cards.body: For das-words, in das becomes ins, an das becomes ans, auf das becomes aufs (Wohin?). The dative shrinks too: in dem becomes im, an dem becomes am (Wo?). But auf dem stays two words. der-words and die-words do not shrink.

examples.en: The plant stands at the window.

examples.de: Ich stelle die Pflanze ans Fenster.
examples.en: I put the plant at the window.

examples.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Regal.
examples.en: The book lies on the shelf.

examples.de: Ich lege das Buch aufs Regal.
examples.en: I lay the book on the shelf.

examples.de: Ich lege das Kissen aufs Sofa.
examples.en: I lay the cushion on the sofa.
examples.why: das Kissen (cushion); Wohin? auf das = aufs.

cards.more: It is like text messages. Instead of in das you write ins. Step 1: is the noun a das-word, like Zimmer, Fenster or Regal? Step 2: if it moves (Wohin?), use ins, ans, aufs. Step 3: if it just sits there (Wo?), use im, am, auf dem. Step 4: for der-words and die-words, nothing shrinks: in den Flur, in die Küche. Extra example: Ich lege das Kissen aufs Sofa.

deeper.text: aufs sounds a little casual. In careful writing you can also say auf das, and people often say it when they want to stress das. Both are right. You will hear ins, ans and aufs all the time, so learn them as the short forms of in das, an das and auf das.

example.en: We go into the living room.

cards.title: Moving-day commands
cards.lead: You can describe where things go. On this card you turn it into the short commands you really shout on moving day, using the du-command from chapter 8.
cards.body: Use the du-command without -st: Stell die Kiste ins Wohnzimmer! Leg den Teppich auf den Boden! Häng das Bild an die Wand! Trag den Karton in die Küche! Ask with Wohin stellst du …? Be polite with Sie: Stellen Sie die Kiste ins Wohnzimmer!
steps: 1. Take the du-form: du stellst, du legst, du hängst, du trägst.
2. Drop -st, and keep the stem: stell, leg, häng, trag.
3. Add the thing and the place with the accusative: die Kiste ins Wohnzimmer.

examples.en: Put the box in the living room!

examples.de: Leg den Teppich auf den Boden!
examples.en: Lay the carpet on the floor!

examples.de: Trag den Karton in die Küche!
examples.en: Carry the box into the kitchen!
examples.why: tragen: Trag! The a stays a.

examples.why: Wohin? asks for the accusative answer.

examples.en: The move is on Saturday.
examples.why: der Umzug = the move to a new home.

examples.en: Tidy up the hall!

cards.more: A command is the verb on its own. Step 1: take the du-form, du stellst, and drop the -st: stell. Step 2: add what you want to move: die Kiste. Step 3: add where it goes: ins Wohnzimmer. Step 4: finish with an exclamation mark. With tragen the a stays: Trag den Karton! (not Träg). Extra example: Leg das Kissen aufs Sofa!

deeper.text: Commands to someone you do not know use Sie, and the verb comes first: Stellen Sie die Kiste bitte ins Wohnzimmer! With friends you use the short du-command. A friendly bitte makes both sound polite. The case after the place word does not change: it is still the accusative, because you are still asking Wohin?

example.de: Stellen Sie die Kiste bitte ins Wohnzimmer!
example.en: Please put the box in the living room!

cards.title: Wo steht es? Wohin stelle ich es?
cards.lead: You have both questions now. On this last card you mix them in one short conversation, as you would on moving day, so you can pick the right case without thinking.
cards.body: In a conversation a person asks Wo? and you answer with a place, or someone asks Wohin? and you answer with a place and the accusative. The verb is steht for Wo? and stelle or stell for Wohin?. Say it aloud: Wo steht der Sessel? Im Wohnzimmer. Wohin stelle ich den Sessel? Ans Fenster.

examples.en: Where is the armchair standing?
It stands in the living room.
Where do I put the armchair?
Put it at the window!
examples.why: Answer to Wohin?: accusative (ans). ihn = der Sessel.

examples.en: There is no space in the hall.
examples.why: der Platz = space; kein Platz = no space.

cards.more: Pretend you are on the phone with Anna. Anna: Wo steht der Sessel? You look at the room and answer with im: it is already there, so Wo and dative. Anna: Wohin stelle ich den Sessel? Now you tell her to move it, so Wohin and accusative: ans Fenster. Step 1: listen for Wo or Wohin. Step 2: look at the verb: steht or stelle. Step 3: answer with the matching case. Extra: Wo liegt das Kissen? Auf dem Sofa.

deeper.text: You can give a very short answer. To Wo? you say Im Wohnzimmer. To Wohin? you say Ans Fenster. The question word and the short form already tell the listener everything. This is how people really talk on a moving day: fast, short, and with the right case.

lessons.goal: Name nine colours, give an opinion about a room, and accept or decline an invitation to see a flat.

grammar.point: A colour after sein takes no ending (Das Sofa ist grün). finden + thing + adjective gives an opinion (Ich finde das Zimmer schön); finden: finde, findest, findet, finden, findet, finden.

cards.title: Before we start: what colour is it?
cards.body: A friend shows you her new flat. What colour is the sofa? Do you like the room? Maybe she asks you to come on Saturday. Today you name colours, give your opinion with finden, and say yes or no to an invitation, all with words you can already build sentences with.
steps: You already know: Die Wohnung ist hell (lesson 2), and that an adjective after sein never changes (chapter 3).
New today: colour words work exactly like that, and finden lets you say what you think: Ich finde das Zimmer schön.
By the end you can: name nine colours, say what you think of a room, and accept or politely decline an invitation.

examples.en: The flat is bright.
examples.why: You know this already. sein + adjective, no ending.

examples.en: The sofa is green.
examples.why: New today: a colour is just an adjective, so it also has no ending.

examples.en: I think the sofa is nice.
examples.why: New today: finden says what you think.

cards.more: Think of a box of crayons. Each crayon is one colour word: rot, blau, grün. You do not change the crayon when you use it. You just say Das Sofa ist grün, like you say Die Wohnung ist hell. The second tool today is the little verb finden, which means to find or to think. You say what you find, and then you say how it is: Ich finde das Zimmer schön. At the end you add a polite yes or no to an invitation. Three small tools, one calm step at a time.

cards.title: The colours
cards.lead: The intro said colours work like any adjective. First you need the words, so on this card you meet nine colour words and a thing for each, to make them stick.
cards.body: Nine colours to learn today: rot, blau, grün, gelb, schwarz, weiß, braun, grau, bunt. Bunt means many colours at once. The colour words are adjectives, so you will use them with sein: Die Tasche ist rot.

examples.en: The bag is red.
The carpet is grey.
The wall is white.
examples.why: weiß = white. ß is a long s.

cards.more: Make a picture for every colour. Rot is a tomato, blau is the sky, grün is grass, gelb is the sun, schwarz is the night, weiß is milk, braun is chocolate, grau is a rainy cloud, bunt is a box of crayons. Step 1: say the colour. Step 2: see the picture. Step 3: say a sentence: Das Kissen ist gelb. Say each one out loud once.

deeper.text: Bunt is a little different: it does not name one colour but many at the same time, like a box of crayons or a flower bed. German often says Das Bild ist bunt when it has lots of colours. Remember ß in weiß: it is just a double s, and the word sounds like vice.

example.en: The picture is colourful.

cards.title: Das Sofa ist grün: no ending
cards.lead: You have the colour words. On this card you use them in a sentence with sein, and you learn that they never change, plus how to make light and dark colours.
cards.body: A colour after sein has no ending: Das Sofa ist grün. Die Sofas sind grün. For many things the verb is sind, but the colour stays the same. Add hell- or dunkel- in front for light and dark: hellblau, dunkelgrün. Write it as one word.

examples.en: The sofa is green.
The cushions are colourful.
examples.why: Plural: sind. The colour stays bunt.

examples.en: The wall is light blue.
The cupboard is dark green.

cards.more: A colour is like a sticker. You stick it after ist or sind and it does not change shape. Step 1: say the thing: Das Sofa. Step 2: say ist (or sind for more than one). Step 3: say the colour, without any ending. Step 4: want it lighter or darker? Put hell or dunkel in front, as one word. Wrong: Das Sofa ist grüne. Right: Das Sofa ist grün.

deeper.text: To ask about a colour, Germans say Welche Farbe hat das Sofa? (What colour does the sofa have?), with haben, not sein. The answer goes back to sein: Das Sofa ist grün. With hell and dunkel the colour stays glued as one word with a small letter: hellblau, dunkelgrau.

example.en: What colour is the carpet?

cards.title: Wie findest du das Zimmer?
cards.lead: You can say what colour things are. Next you learn the verb finden, so you can ask and say what you think about a room, a sofa or a flat.
cards.body: finden means to find, and also to think. Wie findest du das Zimmer? asks for an opinion. Answer: Ich finde das Zimmer schön, or short: Ich finde es schön. After finden comes the thing (accusative) and then the adjective, with no ending.

examples.en: How do you find the room?
I find the room nice.
examples.why: thing first, adjective last, no ending.

examples.en: I find it nice.
Mira thinks the kitchen is great.

cards.more: Finden works like a question and a small judgement. Step 1: ask Wie findest du …? and say the thing. Step 2: answer Ich finde, then the thing, then the adjective. Step 3: use es for a das-word if you do not want to say the noun again: Ich finde es schön. Step 4: the verb has e between d and t: du findest, er findet, like arbeiten. Extra example: Mira findet die Küche super.

deeper.text: In English we say I think the room is nice. German says I find the room nice, with no is. This is why the adjective stands at the end with no ending and no sein. The same verb also means to find a lost thing, as in Ich finde mein Handy, but then there is no adjective.

example.en: I find my phone.

cards.title: An opinion with aber, zu and sehr
cards.lead: You can ask and give an opinion in one short sentence. On this card you make it richer with aber, zu and sehr, so your opinion has a reason and a strength.
cards.body: Join two opinions with aber: Das Zimmer ist hell, aber klein. Make an adjective stronger with sehr (very) or say it is too much with zu. Ich finde die Wohnung zu dunkel. Ich finde den Teppich sehr schön.
steps: 1. Say the thing and an adjective: Das Zimmer ist hell.
2. Add aber and the second part: aber klein.
3. Or use finden with zu or sehr: Ich finde die Wohnung zu dunkel.

examples.de: Das Zimmer ist hell, aber klein.
examples.en: The room is bright, but small.
examples.why: aber joins a good and a bad thing.

examples.de: Ich finde die Wohnung zu dunkel.
examples.en: I find the flat too dark.

examples.de: Ich finde den Teppich sehr schön.
examples.en: I find the carpet very nice.

examples.de: Die Küche ist klein, aber sie ist super.
examples.en: The kitchen is small, but it is great.
examples.why: After aber, a new sentence with its own verb.

cards.more: An opinion has a strength and a reason. Step 1: pick your adjective: hell, klein, dunkel. Step 2: add a strength. sehr means very, and it is positive. zu means too much, and it is a problem. Step 3: contrast with aber if you have a good thing and a bad thing. Extra example: Die Küche ist klein, aber sie ist super.

deeper.text: Notice that aber starts a new part but does not move the verb: the verb stays in second place in the part after aber. Also, German puts a comma before aber. It is a good habit to use aber when you want to be polite: first something nice, then the problem.

example.de: Die Wohnung ist klein, aber ich finde sie schön.
example.en: The flat is small, but I think it is nice.

cards.title: Invite someone: Komm doch vorbei!
cards.lead: You can describe a flat. Now you invite someone to see it. On this card you learn the friendly questions and the chunk Komm doch vorbei!, which you can use right away.
cards.body: Ask Kommst du am Samstag? or Hast du am Samstag Zeit? Then invite with the chunk Komm doch vorbei! It means Come over! Learn it as one piece. doch makes it friendly. vorbeikommen is a separable verb (chapter 6), so vorbei goes to the end.
steps: 1. Ask: Kommst du am Samstag?
2. Invite: Komm doch vorbei!
3. Say the time or day if you like: am Samstag, um vier Uhr.

examples.en: Are you coming on Saturday?
examples.why: A yes/no question starts with the verb.

examples.en: Do you have time on Saturday?
Come over! (Come by!)
examples.why: A chunk. Learn it as one piece.

cards.more: An invitation has three tiny moves. Step 1: ask when: Kommst du am Samstag? Step 2: invite: Komm doch vorbei! Step 3: wait for the answer. It is built like the separable verbs from chapter 6: vorbeikommen, so vorbei jumps to the end. It is the German way to say Come by, you are welcome. Extra example: Hast du am Sonntag Zeit?

deeper.text: Doch is a small friendly word. It softens the command, like please or why not in English. You could say Komm vorbei! but Komm doch vorbei! sounds warmer. It works with every separable verb from chapter 6: Komm doch mit! Ruf mich doch an! doch stands right after the verb, or after a short word like mich.

example.en: Do come along!

cards.title: Say yes or no politely
cards.lead: You can send an invitation. Now the other side: on this card you learn how to say yes with gern and how to say no kindly, with leider and a reason.
cards.body: Yes: Ja, gern! or Danke, ich komme gern. No: Leider kann ich nicht. Add a reason with müssen: Ich muss arbeiten. The friend can answer Schade! Use leider (unfortunately) to be polite when you say no.

rows: Leider kann ich am Samstag nicht.

examples.en: Yes, gladly!
Thanks, I would love to come.

examples.de: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
examples.en: Unfortunately I cannot. I have to work.
examples.why: Leider + können, then a reason with müssen.

examples.de: Leider kann ich am Samstag nicht.
examples.en: Unfortunately I cannot on Saturday.
examples.why: The day can come before nicht.

cards.more: Saying no is easier in German with two small helpers. Step 1: start with leider, which means unfortunately. It sounds sorry, not rude, like a soft cushion before the bad news. Step 2: say kann ich nicht (from können). Step 3: give a short reason with muss: Ich muss arbeiten. Saying yes is shorter: Ja, gern! (gern = with pleasure). If you only say Nein, it sounds hard in German too. Extra example: Leider kann ich am Samstag nicht.

deeper.text: You know können and müssen from chapter 5. In a polite no they work together: können says what is not possible, müssen gives the reason. leider can also stand after the verb: Ich kann leider nicht. Both orders are correct and very common. The other person answers Schade! (Too bad!).

example.en: Unfortunately I cannot.

cards.title: A short invitation dialogue
cards.lead: You have all the pieces now. On this last card you put them together in a short dialogue: an invitation, an answer and a reason, the way a real talk goes.
cards.body: Build a short dialogue with three moves. First the invitation: Kommst du am Sonntag? Komm doch vorbei! Then the answer: Ja, gern! or Leider kann ich nicht. Then the reason or the time: Ich muss arbeiten. Ich komme um drei Uhr.
steps: 1. Invite: Kommst du am Sonntag? Komm doch vorbei!
2. Answer: Ja, gern! or Leider kann ich nicht.
3. Add: um drei Uhr, or Ich muss arbeiten.

examples.de: Kommst du am Sonntag? Komm doch vorbei!
examples.en: Are you coming on Sunday? Come over!

examples.de: Ja, gern! Ich komme um drei Uhr.
examples.en: Yes, gladly! I come at three.
examples.why: Move 2 and 3: yes and a time.

examples.de: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
examples.en: Unfortunately I cannot. I have to work.
examples.why: Move 2 and 3: no and a reason.

cards.more: A talk is a ping-pong game. Step 1: A throws the invitation. Step 2: B throws back yes or no. Step 3: B adds a reason (for no) or a time (for yes). Step 4: A answers with Schade! or Super! Practise it with a friend and swap the roles. Extra example: Ja, gern! Ich komme am Samstag um vier Uhr.

deeper.text: When the answer is yes, the next question is often about the time: Wann denn? or Um wie viel Uhr? (chapter 5). Then you agree: Um drei? Super! If the day does not work, offer another one: Und am Sonntag? One question, one answer and one reason are enough at A1.

example.de: Um wie viel Uhr? Um drei?
example.en: At what time? At three?

lessons.title: Meine Wohnung beschreiben: Text aus Bausteinen
lessons.goal: Build a short text about your home from sentence chunks (place, rooms, furniture, opinion, invitation).

grammar.point: Build a short text in four blocks: place, rooms, furniture with Wo?, opinion and invitation. The verb stays in second place (also after a place or time word); und, aber, zuerst, dann link the parts; separable einziehen and vorbeikommen put the prefix at the end.
grammar.oneLine: Im Wohnzimmer steht ein Sofa. Ich ziehe im Mai ein.

mistake.why: einziehen is a separable verb: the prefix ein goes to the end of the sentence.

terms.meaning: place, rooms, furniture with Wo?, opinion and invitation
separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
words for how a home feels

cards.title: Before we start: tell a friend about your new flat
cards.body: Your friend asks: How is your new flat? You want to say where it is, which rooms it has, what stands where, what you think of it, and that she should come. There is no new rule today. You learn to build one short text from the chunks you already have.
steps: You already know: places and furniture (lessons 3 to 7), colours and opinions (lesson 8), and und, aber, zuerst, dann (chapter 7).
New today: a plan with four blocks that turns many small sentences into one text, plus the separable verbs einziehen and vorbeikommen.
By the end you can: write a message of about 40 words to a friend that describes your home and invites her.

examples.en: There is a sofa in the living room.
examples.why: You know this already: place first, then the verb in second place.

examples.de: Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum, und im Wohnzimmer steht ein Sofa.
examples.en: The flat is in the centre, and in the living room there is a sofa.
examples.why: New today: und chains two sentences into a text.

cards.more: Think of building blocks. Each sentence you know is one block: Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum is a block, Ich finde die Wohnung schön is a block. Alone they are small. Put them in a good order and you have a house: first where it is, then the rooms, then the furniture, then what you think and the invitation. You are not learning new blocks today. You are learning the plan for the house. Every step comes in the next cards.

cards.title: Four blocks for a text
cards.lead: You have many separate chunks from this chapter. On this card you see the order that turns them into one text, so you always know what to say next.
cards.body: A short text about your home has four blocks in this order: 1 Lage (where is the flat?), 2 Zimmer (which rooms?), 3 Möbel und Wo? (what stands where?), 4 Meinung und Einladung (what do you think, who comes?). Every block is two or three short chunks.

rows: Ich finde die Wohnung schön. Komm doch vorbei!

examples.en: The flat is in the centre.

examples.de: Die Wohnung hat zwei Zimmer und einen Balkon.
examples.en: The flat has two rooms and a balcony.
There is a bed in the bedroom.
I find the flat nice.

cards.more: The plan is a little tour. Step 1: stand outside and say where the flat is. Step 2: open the door and name the rooms. Step 3: walk through and say what stands where. Step 4: sit down and say what you think, then invite your friend. Every time you are stuck, ask the next block question. You never have to invent a whole text at once.

deeper.text: A text sounds better when you do not repeat the same noun. After the first sentence, use a pronoun from lesson 1: sie for die Wohnung, er for der Balkon, es for das Bad. Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum. Sie hat zwei Zimmer. Short, clear, and the reader still knows what you mean.

example.de: Die Wohnung ist hell. Sie hat zwei Zimmer.
example.en: The flat is bright. It has two rooms.

cards.title: Block 1: where is the flat?
cards.lead: You know the plan. Now block 1, the first thing a friend asks: where is it? On this card you learn the chunks that describe the place of a flat.
cards.body: Describe the place with small sentences: Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum. Die Lage ist zentral. Die Wohnung ist ruhig. Die Aussicht ist schön. Use lesson 6 to say the type: in einem Hochhaus, in der Stadt, auf dem Land. Lage means location, Aussicht means view.

rows: The flat is in the centre.
in einem Hochhaus, in der Stadt, auf dem Land
in a tower block, in the town, in the countryside

examples.en: The flat is in the centre.
The location is central.
The view is nice.

examples.de: Die Wohnung ist in einem Hochhaus.
examples.en: The flat is in a tower block.

cards.more: The place of a flat is like an address in words. Step 1: say the part of town: im Zentrum, in der Stadt, auf dem Land. Step 2: say the quality of the place with sein: zentral, ruhig. Step 3: add the view if it is nice: Die Aussicht ist schön. Step 4: say the type of house if you like: in einem Hochhaus. Every part is a short sentence with sein.

deeper.text: Natives often use liegen for the location: Die Wohnung liegt zentral or Die Wohnung liegt im Zentrum. Both mean the same as ist im Zentrum. When you look at a flat, people also ask Wie ist die Lage? and answer with one word: Super! or Sehr ruhig. Lage is one of the first things Germans ask about.

example.en: The flat is centrally located.

cards.title: Chain sentences: und, aber, zuerst, dann
cards.lead: You can describe the place. On this card you link your sentences with words from chapter 7, so your text flows from one idea to the next instead of being a list.
cards.body: Link ideas with und (adds), aber (contrasts), zuerst and dann (order). The verb stays in second place in every part. If a place starts the sentence, the verb is still second: Im Wohnzimmer steht ein Sofa. Put a comma before aber. Before und a comma is optional when a whole new sentence follows.

rows: Das Bad ist klein, und die Küche ist hell.
Die Küche ist klein, aber hell.
Zuerst der Flur, dann die Küche.

examples.de: Im Wohnzimmer steht ein Sofa, und im Schlafzimmer steht ein Bett.
examples.en: There is a sofa in the living room, and there is a bed in the bedroom.
examples.why: und adds a second idea. The place comes first, the verb is second.

examples.de: Die Küche ist klein, aber sie ist hell.
examples.en: The kitchen is small, but it is bright.
examples.why: aber contrasts. Each part has a verb.

examples.de: Zuerst gehen wir in den Flur. Dann gehen wir in die Küche.
examples.en: First we go into the hall. Then we go into the kitchen.
examples.why: Time word first, verb second, subject after the verb.

cards.more: The four linking words are glue. Und sticks two ideas side by side. Aber sticks a good thing and a bad thing together. Zuerst and dann put them in order, like walking through the flat. Step 1: write the first idea. Step 2: choose the glue word. Step 3: write the second idea, with the verb in second place. Extra example: Zuerst gehen wir in den Flur.

deeper.text: und and aber do not take a place in the sentence: after them the normal order follows, subject then verb: aber sie ist hell. zuerst and dann are different: they take place 1, so the verb comes next and the subject after it: dann ist sie hell. Compare the two and listen to the order.

example.de: Die Küche ist klein, aber sie ist hell.
example.en: The kitchen is small, but it is bright.

cards.title: Words for how a home feels
cards.lead: You have the chain. On this card you add four words for the feeling of a home, so your opinion block says more than only schön.
cards.body: Four words to describe a home with sein or finden: gemütlich (cosy), sauber (clean), praktisch (practical), zentral (central). No ending: Die Wohnung ist gemütlich. Ich finde die Wohnung gemütlich. Also useful: Das Bad ist in Ordnung (it is fine).

examples.en: The flat is clean.
The kitchen is practical.
I find the living room cosy.

examples.de: Die Wohnung ist gemütlich, aber klein.
examples.en: The flat is cosy, but small.

cards.more: Each word is a small feeling. Gemütlich is the feeling of a warm blanket and a cup of tea. Sauber is a clean kitchen. Praktisch means that things work well. Zentral means that everything is near. Step 1: pick the word that fits your home. Step 2: use sein or finden. Step 3: add sehr if you like it. Extra example: Ich finde die Küche praktisch.

deeper.text: Gemütlich is a word that is hard to translate. It is the feeling of being warm, safe and relaxed in a room, a feeling Germans value a lot. You say it about rooms, flats and evenings. It is one of the most typical German words, and it never gets an ending after sein or finden.

example.en: The room is very cosy.

cards.title: Separable verbs: einziehen and vorbeikommen
cards.lead: You can describe the home. On this card you learn two verbs you need for the story of a move: einziehen and vorbeikommen. Both are separable verbs, which you know from chapter 6.
cards.body: einziehen means to move in, vorbeikommen means to come by. Both are separable: the main part is in second place, the prefix goes to the end. Ich ziehe im Mai ein. Komm am Samstag vorbei! With a modal the whole verb stays together: Ich will im Mai einziehen. Besuch means visitors.

examples.en: I move in in May.
examples.why: The prefix ein goes to the end.

examples.en: Come by on Saturday!
examples.why: A command: prefix at the end.

examples.en: I have visitors on Sunday.
I want to move in in May.
examples.why: With a modal the verb stays whole.

cards.more: A separable verb is like a pair of shoes that you put on separate places. Step 1: find the two parts: ein + ziehen, vorbei + kommen. Step 2: put the main part (ziehe, komm) where the verb belongs, in second place. Step 3: put the little prefix (ein, vorbei) at the very end. Step 4: with a modal, keep the whole infinitive at the end. Extra example: Anna zieht heute ein.

deeper.text: The prefix at the end is the only trick. If you forget it, the sentence has no meaning: Ich ziehe im Mai is incomplete, because the reader waits for ein. Think of the prefix as the end of the sentence. Besuch is a funny word: one person or many can be Besuch, and there is no plural to learn here.

example.en: Mira comes by on Sunday.

cards.title: A message to a friend
cards.lead: You have every piece. On this last card you read a full model message of about 40 words, so you can write your own with the same four blocks.
cards.body:
Here is a model text from Mira to Ben. Lieber Ben, im Mai ziehe ich ein. Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum. Sie hat einen Balkon, aber sie ist klein. Im Wohnzimmer steht ein Sofa. Ich finde die Wohnung gemütlich. Komm doch am Samstag vorbei! Viele Grüße
Mira
steps: 1. Greeting: Liebe Mira, or Lieber Ben,
2. Place: Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum.
3. Rooms: Die Wohnung hat einen Balkon.
4. Furniture with Wo?: Im Wohnzimmer steht ein Sofa.
5. Opinion: Ich finde die Wohnung gemütlich.
6. Invitation and goodbye: Komm doch vorbei! Viele Grüße

examples.en: Dear Ben, I move in in May.

examples.de: Sie hat einen Balkon, aber sie ist klein.
examples.en: It has a balcony, but it is small.
There is a sofa in the living room.
Come by on Saturday!
examples.why: Block 4: the invitation. Then the goodbye Viele Grüße, and your name on the next line.

cards.more: Look at the model like a sandwich. The bread is the greeting at the top and the goodbye at the bottom. The filling has the four blocks: place, rooms, furniture and opinion. The sauce is the invitation. Step 1: copy the shape. Step 2: change the details, like the rooms and the furniture. Step 3: read your text aloud once and tick the checklist.

deeper.text: Liebe is for a woman and Lieber for a man: Liebe Mira, Lieber Ben. After the greeting comes a comma, and the next line starts with a small letter, because it is still the same sentence. The goodbye Viele Grüße has no comma, and your name goes on its own line under it.

example.en: Dear Ben, I have a flat now.

reading.title: Mira sucht eine Wohnung

reading.title: Leons Wohnung in Berlin
reading.text: Leon wohnt mit seiner Schwester in einer Wohnung in Berlin. Die Wohnung ist im Zentrum, in einem Hochhaus. Die Küche ist groß und hell. Der Herd steht neben dem Kühlschrank, und die Mikrowelle steht auf dem Kühlschrank. Zwischen dem Herd und der Tür steht ein Tisch. Die Waschmaschine steht im Keller. Das Wohnzimmer ist ziemlich klein, aber nicht dunkel. Das Sofa steht vor dem Fenster, und das Bild hängt über dem Sofa. Die Schwester von Leon hat eine Katze. Die Katze sitzt auf dem Sessel. Leon wohnt nicht bei seinen Eltern. Die Eltern von Leon wohnen in Italien, auf dem Land.

reading.title: Miras Umzug
reading.text: Mira zieht heute ein. Die Wohnung ist neu und im Zentrum. Ben ist auch da. Er trägt die Kisten in die Wohnung. Mira sagt: Stell den Karton ins Schlafzimmer! Ben stellt den Karton ans Fenster. Mira sagt: Nein, Ben! Ins Schlafzimmer, nicht ans Fenster! Das Sofa steht im Wohnzimmer. Es ist grün. Der Teppich ist grau, und die Kissen sind bunt. Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand. Dann stellt sie die Pflanze auf den Tisch. Ben findet die Wohnung gemütlich. Die Küche ist klein, aber sauber. Am Samstag hat Mira Besuch aus Wien. Sie sagt: Komm doch vorbei, Anna! Anna kommt gern. Leon kann leider nicht. Er muss arbeiten.
